articles.headline: Escambia's $47 Million Stormwater Gamble
articles.dek: County commissioners approved the largest drainage bond in local history last month. Now they have to figure out which neighborhoods get fixed first—and which keep flooding.
brief: Escambia County commissioners approved a $47 million stormwater infrastructure bond in June, the largest drainage investment in county history
The bond will fund repairs and upgrades across 23 identified problem areas, but project prioritization remains undetermined with public input sessions scheduled for August
Critics question whether the funding addresses root causes of flooding or merely patches symptoms of decades of development decisions
articles.body:
The water came up fast on Doris Hendricks' street last September. By the time she got home from her shift at Baptist Hospital, Doris Lane—yes, she lives on a street that shares her first name—had turned into a slow-moving creek. Her mailbox stood in eighteen inches of brown water. The crawl space under her 1960s ranch house took on four inches before the rain stopped.

"It wasn't even a hurricane," Hendricks said. "Just a hard afternoon rain. The kind we used to get every summer without this happening."

Hendricks lives in the Brownsville area, one of 23 neighborhoods the county has identified as chronic flooding zones. Last month, Escambia County commissioners voted 4-1 to approve a $47 million bond to address drainage infrastructure failures across the county. It is the largest single investment in stormwater management in local history.

The money exists. The plan does not.

The Prioritization Problem

County Administrator Wes Moreno told commissioners during the June 18 vote that staff would develop a project ranking system over the summer. Public input sessions are scheduled for August. Construction on the first projects could begin by spring 2027.

That timeline assumes agreement on something the county has struggled to define: which neighborhoods need help most, and how you measure that need.

"Do you prioritize by severity of flooding? By number of homes affected? By property values at risk? By how long residents have been waiting?" asked Commissioner Steven Barry during the June meeting. Barry cast the lone dissenting vote, not because he opposed the funding but because he wanted the prioritization framework established before approval.

"We're writing a $47 million check and telling people to trust us," Barry said. "Some of these neighborhoods have been promised fixes for fifteen years."

He's not wrong about the timeline. Residents in the Brentwood neighborhood near the airport first petitioned the county about drainage failures in 2009. The Tanyard Creek watershed study that identified their problems was completed in 2012. Recommended improvements were never funded.

Where the Money Goes

County documents outline the 23 priority areas but provide cost estimates for only seven of them. The Carpenter Creek watershed—which floods portions of the Scenic Heights and Goulding areas—carries the highest preliminary estimate at $8.2 million. The Jones Swamp drainage basin, affecting neighborhoods near West Pensacola, comes in at $6.1 million.

Simple arithmetic creates a problem. If those two projects alone consume $14.3 million, roughly 30 percent of the bond, what happens to the other 21 neighborhoods?

Moreno acknowledged the funding won't address every identified project. "This bond provides significant capacity, but it's not unlimited," he said. "Some projects will require phasing. Others may need to wait for future funding cycles."

Future funding cycles. The phrase appears in county planning documents with regularity. It appeared in the 2012 Tanyard Creek study. It appeared in the 2018 stormwater master plan. It appears in the current bond proposal.

For residents like Hendricks, the phrase has become a kind of shorthand for never.

Development and Drainage

The flooding problems aren't random. They follow patterns that map closely to development decisions made over the past four decades.

Escambia County adopted its first comprehensive stormwater management ordinance in 1991. Before that, developers faced minimal requirements for managing runoff from new construction. Subdivisions built in the 1970s and 1980s—many in the areas now identified as flooding zones—were designed with undersized drainage infrastructure or none at all.

"The chickens are coming home to roost," said Dr. Wade Jeffrey, a professor of environmental science at the University of West Florida who has studied local watershed issues. "Every impervious surface—every roof, every driveway, every parking lot—has to drain somewhere. For decades, the answer was basically 'downhill' without much thought to what happened next."

What happened next, in many cases, was that downhill neighborhoods became collection points for runoff from uphill development.

The Brownsville area sits at the bottom of a drainage basin that includes portions of the Nine Mile Road commercial corridor. When that corridor developed rapidly in the 1990s and 2000s, stormwater that once absorbed into undeveloped land began flowing toward existing neighborhoods.

Hendricks bought her house in 1987. The crawl space flooding started around 2010.

"Nobody told us when we bought here that they were going to pave over everything north of us and send the water our way," she said. "Now I'm supposed to be grateful they're finally going to fix what they broke."

The Skeptics

Not everyone is convinced the bond will fix much of anything.

Jerry Couey has lived in the Ensley area for 31 years. His neighborhood appears on the county's priority list, somewhere in the middle. He attended a county commission meeting in May to speak during public comment.

"I've seen three different drainage studies cover my street," Couey told commissioners. "Each one identified the same problems. Each one recommended fixes. Nothing ever got built. Why should I believe this time is different?"

Commissioner Lumon May, who represents much of the Ensley area, pushed back gently. "This time there's actual money attached," May said. "That's the difference."

Couey wasn't persuaded. "Money to study it more," he said. "Money to plan it more. Call me when somebody shows up with a shovel."

The skepticism extends beyond frustrated residents. Local environmental advocates question whether the bond addresses symptoms rather than causes.

Christian Wagley, who serves on the Pensacola Bay Area Environmental Coalition, argues that the county continues to approve development patterns that worsen drainage problems while simultaneously borrowing money to fix those same problems.

"It's a circular system," Wagley said. "New development generates impact fees and property taxes. That revenue gets used to mitigate the damage the development causes. Meanwhile, the next development gets approved and the cycle continues."

County officials dispute this characterization. Post-1991 development, they note, must meet stormwater standards that older construction didn't face. The current problems, they argue, stem largely from pre-regulation development.

"We can't un-build the last fifty years," Moreno said. "What we can do is address the infrastructure deficits we inherited and ensure new development doesn't create new problems."

What Happens Next

The August public input sessions will take place at locations across the county, though specific dates and venues haven't been announced. Moreno said the county will present preliminary prioritization criteria and solicit feedback before finalizing the project list.

The criteria under consideration include: severity of flooding impact, number of structures affected, frequency of flooding events, cost-effectiveness of proposed solutions, and time since the area was first identified as a problem.

That last criterion could prove contentious. If wait time becomes a significant factor, neighborhoods like Brentwood—first flagged in 2009—would jump ahead of areas with potentially worse current flooding but shorter documented histories.

Commissioner Barry suggested during the June meeting that the county hire an independent consultant to develop the prioritization framework, removing the decision from staff who might face political pressure. The motion failed 3-2.

"I don't think anyone is trying to game this," said Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, who voted against the independent consultant. "But I understand why people might worry about it. This is a lot of money and there are going to be winners and losers."

Hendricks, in Brownsville, has no illusions about which category her street will fall into.

"We're not a squeaky wheel neighborhood," she said. "We don't show up at meetings. We don't have a homeowners association lobbying for us. We just live here and hope somebody remembers we exist."

She's preparing for another rainy season regardless. Last fall, after the September flooding, she paid a contractor $2,400 to install a sump pump in her crawl space. The county offered no assistance.

"That's two months of my car payments," she said. "But I couldn't wait around for them to fix the drainage. The mold doesn't wait."

The $47 million bond will be repaid over 20 years through a combination of existing stormwater utility fees and general fund revenues. The county estimates the debt service will average $3.2 million annually.

Whether Doris Hendricks' street sees a shovel before that debt is retired remains an open question. The county says it's committed. The neighbors have heard that before.

The water, when it comes, doesn't care about either.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The Last Block of Belmont-DeVilliers
articles.dek: A single row of shotgun houses stands between a $12 million mixed-use development and completion. The families who live there aren't selling.
brief: Five families on the 700 block of North DeVilliers Street have refused buyout offers from Coastal Heritage Partners, stalling the final phase of a mixed-use development project
The shotgun houses, some dating to the 1920s, represent the last intact residential block of Pensacola's historic Black business district
City officials say eminent domain is not under consideration, but residents remain skeptical after attending closed-door meetings they were not invited to
articles.body:
The screen door at 718 North DeVilliers Street doesn't close right anymore. Willa Mae Henderson, 79, has to lift it and push with her hip. She's done this maybe ten thousand times since she moved here in 1971, into the shotgun house her husband's grandmother built.

"They want me to leave so they can put up some coffee shop," Henderson said, settling into a metal porch chair that scraped against wood planks worn smooth by generations. "I told them I'll leave when the Lord calls me. Not before."

Henderson is one of five property owners on this block who have declined buyout offers from Coastal Heritage Partners, the Pensacola-based development firm behind the Belmont Revival project. The $12 million mixed-use development has already transformed three surrounding blocks into a collection of restaurants, boutiques, apartments, and office space marketed as a celebration of the neighborhood's history as the Harlem of the South.

The celebration, it turns out, has limits.

A Street Divided

Walk north on DeVilliers from West Gregory Street and the new Pensacola reveals itself in stages. Fresh brick pavers. Native landscaping. A taproom called The Chitlin Circuit where craft beer costs $9 a pint. Loft apartments with rooftop terraces advertised at $1,800 a month.

Then, at the 700 block, the pavers end. The sidewalk returns to cracked concrete and patchy grass. Five shotgun houses sit in a row, wood frames weathered gray, tin roofs rusted at the edges. They are small—maybe 900 square feet each—and they are occupied.

The contrast is so stark it looks intentional, like a museum exhibit about what stood here before.

"That's exactly what they want," said Marcus Williams, 52, who owns the house at 722 North DeVilliers. "They want us to look bad. They stopped maintaining the street. They let the city stop picking up trash regular. They want everybody driving by to think, 'Why don't those people just sell?'"

Williams is a maintenance supervisor at Baptist Hospital. He inherited the house from his mother, who inherited it from hers. Four generations of Williams have been born in the back bedroom.

Coastal Heritage Partners declined multiple interview requests for this story. In a written statement, company spokesperson Dana Whitfield said the firm "remains committed to working collaboratively with all stakeholders to honor the legacy of the Belmont-DeVilliers district while creating economic opportunity for the broader community."

The statement did not address specific buyout offers or future plans for the 700 block.

The Offers

According to documents reviewed by The Flightline, Coastal Heritage Partners made its first written offers to the five homeowners in March 2024. The amounts ranged from $85,000 to $110,000, depending on lot size and assessed condition.

Escambia County property records show the assessed value of these properties ranges from $42,000 to $61,000. The offers represented premiums of 80 to 100 percent above assessed value.

The homeowners weren't impressed.

"Eighty-five thousand dollars," said Patricia Cobb, 67, who lives at 726 North DeVilliers with her adult son. "You know what that buys you in Pensacola now? Nothing. A trailer in Century, maybe. They want to give me trailer money for my family's land."

Cobb's house was built in 1924 by her great-grandfather, Solomon Cobb, a carpenter who helped construct many of the commercial buildings along the corridor during the neighborhood's heyday. She keeps his tools in a shed out back.

By fall 2024, the offers had increased. Documents show amounts between $140,000 and $175,000. Still no takers.

In February 2025, Coastal Heritage Partners sent representatives to each home in person. According to the homeowners, the representatives suggested that remaining in place could become "uncomfortable" as construction continued around them.

"The man sat right there," Henderson said, pointing to a chair on her porch. "Nice suit. Nice smile. He said, 'Mrs. Henderson, have you thought about what it's going to be like with dump trucks going by at six in the morning? With all that dust?'"

She told him she'd survived two husbands, raised four children, and worked thirty years at Sacred Heart cleaning rooms. Dump trucks weren't going to be the thing that broke her.

What the City Knows

Pensacola City Council member Teniadé Broughton, whose District 7 includes the Belmont-DeVilliers area, said she has spoken with both the homeowners and Coastal Heritage Partners representatives multiple times.

"These are incredibly difficult situations," Broughton said in an interview. "You have a development that by most measures has been successful—it's brought jobs, it's brought investment to a historically disinvested area. But you also have families with deep roots who feel like that success is happening around them, not with them."

Broughton confirmed that eminent domain—the government's power to take private property for public use with compensation—is not being considered by the city.

"The city is not going to take anyone's home to facilitate a private development," she said. "That's not on the table."

But several homeowners said they attended a meeting at City Hall in January 2026 where they saw Coastal Heritage Partners executives in a conference room with city staff. They were not invited to participate.

"I went to pay my water bill," Williams said. "And there they were, up on the third floor, all sitting around the big table. I saw the mayor's chief of staff in there. I saw two people from the planning department. I saw the lawyers from Coastal Heritage."

Williams said he asked a receptionist what the meeting was about. He was told it was a routine development consultation and that it was not open to the public.

City spokesperson Amanda Chen said she could not comment on specific meetings but confirmed that city staff "regularly meet with developers, community members, and other stakeholders as part of the normal planning process."

The Flightline filed a public records request for meeting agendas, sign-in sheets, and any correspondence related to the 700 block of North DeVilliers Street. The request remains pending after 47 days.

What Stood Here

Before it was a development opportunity, before it was blighted, before it was neglected, the Belmont-DeVilliers corridor was the commercial and cultural heart of Black Pensacola.

From the 1920s through the 1960s, the district housed more than 100 Black-owned businesses: doctors' offices, law firms, hotels, restaurants, nightclubs. Musicians including Ray Charles, James Brown, and Fats Domino performed here. The Abe Lincoln Theater at Belmont and DeVilliers showed first-run films to segregated audiences.

Integration changed everything. When Black residents gained access to white-owned businesses, many stopped patronizing their own. The businesses closed. The buildings emptied. By the 1980s, the corridor was synonymous with poverty and crime.

Coastal Heritage Partners acquired its first parcels here in 2019. The company's founder, Richard Leland, grew up in East Hill and has described the Belmont Revival project as a personal mission to restore the district's former glory.

"We're not erasing history," Leland said in a 2023 interview with the Pensacola News Journal. "We're bringing it back."

The homeowners on the 700 block see it differently.

"History isn't a building you put a plaque on," Cobb said. "History is people. We're the history. Our families built this place. We stayed when everybody else left. And now they want to push us out so they can sell our history to tourists."

What Happens Next

The final phase of Belmont Revival—a four-story mixed-use building with ground-floor retail and 48 residential units—was originally scheduled to break ground in spring 2026. The project site surrounds the 700 block on three sides.

According to planning documents filed with the city, Coastal Heritage Partners has redesigned the project three times to work around the existing homes. The current design leaves a gap in the building's footprint, creating what one architect's rendering labels a "heritage courtyard" adjacent to the shotgun houses.

The homeowners were not consulted on this design.

"They want to put us in a fishbowl," Williams said. "People sitting at the coffee shop can look at us like we're in a zoo. 'Look at the old houses. Look at the old Black people. Isn't it charming.'"

He walked to the edge of his porch and pointed at the construction fence 30 feet away, where a banner proclaimed: BELMONT REVIVAL: HONORING THE PAST, BUILDING THE FUTURE.

"I'm the past they're honoring," he said. "And they can't wait to get rid of me."

Henderson, next door, said she plans to die in her house. Her children have told her they'll never sell either.

"My husband's grandmother paid $200 for this land in 1922," she said. "Two hundred dollars. She worked as a maid. She saved every penny. And some man in a suit thinks he can wave his checkbook and make that go away."

She lifted the screen door, pushed it with her hip, and went inside. The evening light caught the dust in the air, golden for a moment, before the door closed behind her.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Show Draws Record Crowd, Record Complaints
articles.dek: NAS Pensacola counted 185,000 attendees at last weekend's airshow. Pensacola Beach residents counted something else: three days of gridlock and a sheriff's deputy who told them to 'just stay home.'
brief: NAS Pensacola reports 185,000 attendees over three days, breaking the 2019 record by 12,000
Pensacola Beach residents describe hours-long waits to cross Bob Sikes Bridge, with some unable to reach homes until after 10 p.m.
Escambia County Sheriff's Office acknowledges traffic plan 'needs review' after deputies advised residents to avoid leaving their homes during show hours
articles.body:
Linda Marchand stood on her second-floor balcony Saturday afternoon, watching the Blue Angels carve white lines across a cloudless sky. She'd lived on Ariola Drive for eleven years. She knew the show by heart. What she didn't know was whether she'd make it to her sister's house in Gulf Breeze for dinner.

She didn't. The drive that normally takes twenty minutes took two hours and forty-five.

"I left at 4:30, thinking the worst was over," Marchand said. "I got to Via de Luna and just stopped. Dead stopped. For forty minutes I didn't move at all."

The Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show, held July 10-12 at Naval Air Station Pensacola, drew a record 185,000 spectators over three days, according to base public affairs. That figure surpasses the previous record of 173,000 set in 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic forced two years of cancellations and scaled-back events.

For NAS Pensacola and the Blue Angels, the numbers represent a triumphant return. For residents of Pensacola Beach and the Gulf Breeze peninsula, they represent something else: a traffic management system that buckled under the weight of its own success.

Three Days of Gridlock

The complaints started Friday morning and didn't stop until late Sunday night.

At least two dozen Pensacola Beach residents contacted The Flightline over the weekend, describing similar experiences. Wait times to cross the Bob Sikes Bridge ranged from ninety minutes to over three hours. Some residents reported being unable to return home from work until after 10 p.m. Others said they skipped the beach entirely, staying with friends or family on the mainland.

Tom Reznicek, who owns a home on Ensenada Marbella, said he tried to leave the island Saturday morning for a doctor's appointment in Pensacola.

"I gave myself two hours," Reznicek said. "I missed it by forty minutes. A nine o'clock appointment. I left at seven."

The Bob Sikes Bridge, the only vehicle access point to Pensacola Beach, becomes a chokepoint during any major beach event. But residents said this year felt different—worse, longer, with less communication from authorities about what to expect.

'Just Stay Home'

Several residents described interactions with Escambia County Sheriff's Office deputies that left them frustrated.

Maria Santos, who lives on Avenida 23, said she approached a deputy stationed near the foot of the bridge Saturday afternoon to ask about alternate routes or expected wait times.

"He told me there was nothing he could do," Santos said. "He said, 'If you live out here during the air show, you should just plan to stay home.' Like that was a real answer."

ECSO spokesperson Sgt. Andrew Hobbs confirmed that deputies were stationed at several points along the beach access routes but said their primary role was traffic flow, not resident assistance.

"Our deputies were focused on keeping vehicles moving and preventing accidents," Hobbs said in an email. "We understand residents experienced delays, and we'll be reviewing our traffic management plan with county officials before next year's event."

Hobbs declined to say whether the advice to "stay home" reflected official guidance or an individual deputy's remarks.

The Math Problem

The core issue is arithmetic. Pensacola Beach has roughly 2,800 permanent residents, according to Santa Rosa Island Authority estimates. On a busy summer Saturday, the island might see 15,000 to 20,000 visitors. During the air show, the base is three miles across the bay, visible from the beach. The island becomes an unofficial overflow viewing area.

No one counts how many people come to the beach specifically to watch the show. But residents describe a transformation: parking lots full by 9 a.m., beach access points jammed, the two-lane bridge grinding to a halt in both directions.

"It's not the base's fault people want to watch from the beach," said Jim Knudsen, a member of the Pensacola Beach Advocates civic group. "But somebody has to plan for it. Right now, nobody does."

Knudsen said the group has raised traffic concerns with Santa Rosa Island Authority and Escambia County officials for years, with little response.

"We get told it's a three-day inconvenience and we should be proud of our military heritage," Knudsen said. "I am proud. I'm also stuck in my driveway."

The View from the Base

NAS Pensacola public affairs officer Lt. Cmdr. Rachel Torres said the base was "thrilled" with attendance and received "overwhelmingly positive feedback" from spectators.

"The Blue Angels Homecoming is one of the premier events in naval aviation, and the Pensacola community's support makes it possible," Torres said in a statement.

Asked about off-base traffic impacts, Torres said the base coordinates with local law enforcement but that traffic management outside the installation falls to civilian authorities.

Escambia County spokeswoman Laura Coale said the county would conduct an after-action review of traffic operations.

"We're aware of the concerns and we take them seriously," Coale said. "This was a record-breaking event, and we want to make sure our traffic plans keep pace with growth."

She did not provide a timeline for the review or say whether residents would be consulted.

No Easy Fix

The geography of Pensacola Beach limits options. The Bob Sikes Bridge can't be widened without massive investment. There's no secondary access point. During peak traffic, the island simply fills up.

Some residents have suggested timed entry restrictions during major events, similar to systems used at national parks. Others want dedicated resident lanes on the bridge—a logistically complex proposal that would require coordination between Escambia County, the Florida Department of Transportation and the Santa Rosa Island Authority.

For now, residents like Marchand are left with the same advice the deputy gave: plan to stay home.

"I love the Blue Angels," Marchand said. "I moved here partly because of them. But I also need to live my life. I need to get groceries. I need to see my family. Three days a year, I apparently can't do that."

She paused.

"Well, I can. It just takes three hours."
